authors: Marzetta, T. L.
title: Noncooperative cellular wireless with unlimited numbers of base station antennas
contribution: Marzetta derives throughput limits for a multicell time-division duplex array using conjugate processing and reused uplink pilots.
strength: The limiting analysis identifies coherent interference from pilot reuse even as fast fading and uncorrelated noise average away.
limitation: The result takes the array size to infinity under a specified propagation and processing model.
distance: The scheduler evaluates finite-array channel vectors on each tone, where two candidate partners can retain substantial spatial overlap.

authors: Ngo, H. Q., Ashikhmin, A., Yang, H., Larsson, E. G. & Marzetta, T. L.
title: Cell-free massive MIMO versus small cells
contribution: Ngo and colleagues compare distributed cooperative access points with dedicated small cells using matched filtering on the uplink and conjugate beamforming on the downlink.
strength: Closed-form per-user throughput expressions support max–min power control and comparisons of service at the lower tail of the user distribution.
limitation: The throughput comparison assumes a specified access-point architecture and serving rule.
distance: The scheduler chooses which two users share each tone and bounds the sum rate forgone by that particular assignment.

authors: Björnson, E. & Sanguinetti, L.
title: Making cell-free massive MIMO competitive with MMSE processing and centralized implementation
contribution: Björnson and Sanguinetti compare four levels of access-point cooperation for uplink reception under spatially correlated fading.
strength: Their spectral-efficiency and fronthaul comparisons quantify the benefits of centralized MMSE combining in the networks studied.
limitation: Their comparison ranks receiver architectures under a specified user population.
distance: The scheduler keeps its deployed filters fixed in the achievable-rate calculation and lets each alternative pair re-optimize its filters in the upper bound.

authors: Demir, Ö. T., Björnson, E. & Sanguinetti, L.
title: Foundations of user-centric cell-free massive MIMO
contribution: Demir and colleagues formulate user-centric cell-free processing in which each user is served jointly by a selected group of access points.
strength: Their framework relates channel estimation and uplink reception to complexity and fronthaul requirements as the network grows.
limitation: Its scalable cooperation framework limits which access points serve each user and how their observations are processed.
distance: The scheduler takes the available receive dimensions as given and bounds the cost of pairing users on distinct frequencies.

authors: Buzzi, S., D’Andrea, C., Zappone, A. & D’Elia, C.
title: User-centric 5G cellular networks: resource allocation and comparison with the cell-free massive MIMO approach
contribution: Buzzi and colleagues compare serving a mobile from a subset of access points with serving it from the entire cell-free network and develop power-allocation schemes.
strength: Their comparison examines both aggregate throughput and fairness for multi-antenna terminals and access points.
limitation: The evaluated serving rule selects access points for each terminal, with power allocation conditioned on that association.
distance: The discrete choices certified here specify which terminals share a tone and which tone each pair occupies.

authors: Caire, G.
title: On the ergodic rate lower bounds with applications to massive MIMO
contribution: Caire derives two achievable ergodic-rate bounds for settings in which the effective channel may harden weakly.
strength: The analysis explains how coherence length and residual interference affect the tightness of different bounds.
limitation: The bounds concern a rate averaged over channel realizations.
distance: The lower endpoint here concerns the deployed receiver on one channel realization, conditional on the calibrated error event when pilots supply the channel estimate.

authors: Wang, Z., Zhang, J., Ngo, H. Q., Ai, B. & Debbah, M.
title: Uplink precoding design for cell-free massive MIMO with iteratively weighted MMSE
contribution: Wang and colleagues design uplink precoders for multi-antenna users under centralized processing and large-scale fading decoding.
strength: Their iteratively weighted MMSE formulation accommodates weighted sum spectral efficiency with spatially correlated channels.
limitation: The iterative optimization addresses continuous precoders for the two processing architectures.
distance: The scheduler certifies a comparison across discrete user pairings and tone assignments as well as continuous transmit powers.

authors: Haustein, T.
title: Real time signal processing for multi-antenna systems and experimental verification on a reconfigurable hardware test-bed
contribution: Haustein implemented channel-adaptive multi-antenna transmission on a reconfigurable testbed and evaluated uplink scheduling on measured channels.
strength: The hardware experiments link scheduling decisions to the throughput of a working radio.
limitation: The measured throughput is specific to the implemented transmission modes and experimental channels.
distance: The present study replays recorded channel observations and bounds the rate difference between a stored receiver action and competing schedules.

authors: Viterbo, E. & Hottinen, A.
title: Optimal user pairing for multiuser MIMO
venue: Proc. 10th IEEE Int. Symp. Spread Spectrum Tech. Appl. (ISSSTA)
contribution: Viterbo and Hottinen formulated uplink user pairing as a combinatorial assignment and compared MMSE and maximum-likelihood detection.
strength: Their equal-energy scheduling window isolates the gain from selecting spatially compatible partners.
limitation: Pair scores depend on the users’ channels and do not change with a separately assigned frequency label in that model.
distance: The present four-user example makes pair values tone-dependent and exhibits a positive gap even after optimizing tone prices.

authors: Fan, J., Li, G. Y., Yin, Q., Peng, B. & Zhu, X.
title: Joint user pairing and resource allocation for LTE uplink transmission
contribution: Fan and colleagues optimized linear-MMSE user pairing and contiguous resource-block allocation in the LTE uplink.
strength: Branch-and-bound gives an exact discrete benchmark for their lower-complexity scheduling procedures.
limitation: The pair scores use prescribed user powers and an SC-FDMA rate calculated after despreading.
distance: Here one labelled tone serves each pair, and the upper bound covers every power allocation within the individual and total power constraints.

authors: Ruder, M. A., Ding, D., Dang, U. L., Vasilakos, A. V. & Gerstacker, W. H.
title: Joint user grouping and frequency allocation for multiuser SC-FDMA transmission
contribution: Ruder and colleagues jointly selected user groups and frequency chunks for an SC-FDMA uplink using capacity or receiver-dependent bit-error-rate metrics, including linear-MMSE and successive-cancellation receivers.
strength: They give exact small-instance benchmarks by full enumeration, identify Blossom matching for time-domain pairing and extend frequency-domain scheduling to groups larger than two.
limitation: The frequency-domain heuristic alternates Hungarian assignments with user swaps under fixed equal powers and perfect channel knowledge; its convergence does not guarantee a globally optimal grouping.
distance: Here a general-graph matching relaxation supplies a checkable upper bound for tone-dependent pairing with continuous powers, without requiring exact labelled enumeration.

authors: Ruder, M. A., Moldovan, A. & Gerstacker, W. H.
title: SC-FDMA user pairing and frequency allocation with imperfect channel state information
contribution: Ruder and colleagues derived MMSE interpolation and prediction filters and channel-acquisition MSE expressions for LTE sounding, then studied their effect on SC-FDMA pairing and frequency allocation.
strength: Their simulations compare scheduling algorithms with a perfect-CSI full-search benchmark for eight users and six resource blocks and show how mobility can erase the gain over random allocation.
limitation: Transmit powers are fixed and equal, and the simulations assume known user velocities and channel statistics plus perfect CSI for payload detection and equalization.
distance: Here held-out calibration bounds errors both for competing receive directions and for the stored filters of the implemented decision.

authors: Prasad, N., Zhang, H., Zhu, H. & Rangarajan, S.
title: Multi-user MIMO scheduling in the fourth generation cellular uplink
contribution: Prasad and colleagues formulated LTE-Advanced uplink scheduling as submodular maximization subject to matroid and knapsack constraints.
strength: Alongside constant-factor approximation guarantees, the paper provides a greedy-solution-dependent upper bound and an upper bound obtained by relaxing power allocation and enumerating precoders.
limitation: These two benchmarking upper bounds are derived for the case without knapsack constraints and retain the paper's weighted-rate objective and receiver model.
distance: Here an additive interval bounds the loss of a full-service, two-user-per-tone action evaluated with its implemented linear receive filters under calibrated channel uncertainty.

authors: Viswanath, P., Tse, D. N. C. & Anantharam, V.
title: Asymptotically optimal water-filling in vector multiple-access channels
contribution: Viswanath and colleagues derived an asymptotically optimal water-filling rule for sum capacity in fading vector multiple-access channels with random signal directions.
strength: The limiting allocation depends on each user's instantaneous fading amplitude in the CDMA model and its slow-fading component in the multiantenna model.
limitation: The optimality result concerns a joint limit in users and signal dimensions under the paper’s channel assumptions.
distance: Here finite channel vectors determine which two users share each tone and a separate linear receiver treats their mutual interference explicitly.

authors: Shi, S., Schubert, M. & Boche, H.
title: Rate optimization for multiuser MIMO systems with linear processing
contribution: Shi and colleagues optimized weighted sum rate and minimum user rate by alternating power allocation and linear transceiver updates.
strength: An MSE-based geometric program provides the power update and the authors prove monotonic convergence.
limitation: Monotonic objective improvement gives no numerical upper bound on the remaining global weighted-sum-rate gain.
distance: The present calculation uses optimized linear directions for the oracle while evaluating the stored directions of the proposed action.

authors: Shen, K. & Yu, W.
title: Fractional programming for communication systems—Part I: Power control and beamforming
contribution: Shen and Yu introduced a quadratic transform for continuous optimization with multiple fractional terms, including power control and beamforming.
strength: The transformation gives tractable updates for coupled signal-to-interference ratios with convergence to a stationary point under the stated assumptions.
limitation: Stationarity alone leaves the difference between the attained objective and its global optimum undetermined.
distance: The power enclosures here bound competing continuous powers even when the implemented powers come from a suboptimal proposal.

authors: Shen, K. & Yu, W.
title: Fractional programming for communication systems—Part II: Uplink scheduling via matching
contribution: Shen and Yu decoupled intercell interference so that coordinated uplink scheduling could alternate matching with continuous power or beamforming updates.
strength: Matching handles discrete assignments directly in a distributed iteration with a convergence guarantee.
limitation: Optimality of a matching update is conditional on the other variables at that iteration.
distance: The matching in the present study instead bounds all schedules after relaxing the requirement that different pairs use different tones.

authors: Sun, H. et al.
title: Learning to optimize: training deep neural networks for interference management
contribution: A feed-forward network approximates the input–output map of WMMSE power control.
strength: The authors quantify approximation complexity and demonstrate fast inference on synthetic wireless and measured DSL channels.
limitation: Agreement with WMMSE measures fidelity to an iterative teacher that can stop at a stationary point.
distance: An individual schedule requires an upper endpoint over all alternatives in addition to its achieved rate.

authors: Shen, Y., Shi, Y., Zhang, J. & Letaief, K. B.
title: Graph neural networks for scalable radio resource management: architecture design and theoretical analysis
contribution: Message-passing graph networks exploit permutation symmetry in radio resource allocation.
strength: Shared local updates allow a policy trained at one network size to operate on larger networks.
limitation: Permutation equivariance constrains how reindexing changes the output but leaves its distance to the global optimum unspecified.
distance: A learned schedule or price enters the uplink comparison only after its feasibility or bound has been checked.

authors: Hejazi, P. & Sabaei, M.
title: Optimizing spectral efficiency through user clustering in user-centric cell-free massive MIMO environment for 6G wireless network
contribution: Hejazi and Sabaei jointly selected user clusters and serving base stations in a cell-free model using non-orthogonal access and successive interference cancellation.
strength: A supervised ensemble trained on solver outputs provides candidate assignments for the coupled clustering and association decisions.
limitation: Classification and throughput results for rounded network outputs do not bound their instance-specific distance from the optimum.
distance: The present paper verifies a feasible decision under separate linear receive filters and supplies a rate upper bound over all competing labelled pairs and powers.

authors: Ahmadi, N. & Akbarizadeh, G.
title: Machine learning based power control in cellular and cell-free massive MIMO systems
contribution: The authors evaluated neural power control against weighted minimum mean-square error optimization in cellular and cell-free massive MIMO.
strength: They compared per-user spectral-efficiency distributions and execution times across different antenna, access-point and user counts.
limitation: The reference policy is an iterative WMMSE power allocator whose output need not attain a global optimum.
distance: Agreement with WMMSE on a population leaves the loss of an individual joint pairing, tone and power decision undetermined.

authors: Hamakawa, Y., Kashimata, T., Yamasaki, M. & Tatsumura, K.
title: Machine learning-assisted high-speed combinatorial optimization with Ising machines for dynamically changing problems
contribution: The authors used learned parameter settings and a hardware Ising solver to find independent sets for successive TDMA scheduling problems in wireless multihop networks.
strength: The demonstration included the cost of transferring each changing problem to the solver when assessing scheduling speed.
limitation: The demonstration minimizes TDMA slots by repeatedly solving independent-set subproblems on conflict graphs.
distance: The paired uplink instead assigns tones and continuous powers and bounds the rate available to every competing decision.

authors: Kashimata, T., Hamakawa, Y., Yamasaki, M. & Tatsumura, K.
title: Real-time black-box optimization for dynamic discrete environments using embedded Ising machines
contribution: A hardware-assisted optimizer used throughput feedback to choose beam directions and discrete power levels for cochannel cells with moving users.
strength: The experiments compared total-throughput feedback with 37 per-base-station sub-rewards, and multi-reward modeling improved tracking performance as users moved in the simulator.
limitation: The wireless evaluation coupled the controller to simulated propagation and assessed average reward across successive actions.
distance: The paired-uplink certificate compares a single implemented schedule with alternatives on the same channel.

authors: Dinitz, M., Im, S., Lavastida, T., Moseley, B. & Vassilvitskii, S.
title: Faster matchings via learned duals
contribution: The authors repair predicted dual variables and warm-start an exact primal–dual algorithm for weighted bipartite matching and b-matching.
strength: Their running-time analysis relates the work needed to the error in the predicted dual variables.
limitation: The bipartite problem has two vertex classes and given edge weights.
distance: Pairing two users requires a general-graph witness, and the price assigned to each edge must also bound continuous powers across tones.

authors: Bessa, S., Dabert, D., Bourgeat, M., Rousseau, L.-M. & Cappart, Q.
title: Learning valid dual bounds in constraint programming: boosted Lagrangian decomposition with self-supervised learning
contribution: A self-supervised network predicts Lagrangian multipliers for decomposed constraint programs inside tree search.
strength: On multidimensional knapsack and shift-scheduling instances, evaluating the learned multipliers retained valid dual bounds and reduced the search time.
limitation: The reported gains depend on decompositions into the constraint-programming subproblems used in those benchmarks.
distance: Here a learned price may initialize the bound, while continuous-power enclosures and the rate of a feasible fixed receiver determine the scheduling interval.

authors: Edmonds, J.
title: Maximum matching and a polyhedron with 0,1-vertices
venue: J. Res. Natl Bur. Stand. B
contribution: Edmonds describes the matching polytope of a general graph using degree and odd-set inequalities.
strength: Its integral vertices permit linear optimization over matchings and dual witnesses for the optimum.
limitation: An edge in the matching problem has a fixed weight and carries no obligation to use a distinct tone.
distance: The odd-set witness certifies the relaxed pairing objective after power and tone enclosures supply edge weights.

authors: Kuhn, H. W.
title: The Hungarian method for the assignment problem
contribution: The Hungarian method computes an optimal one-to-one assignment from a score matrix.
strength: It resolves competition for columns exactly for a fixed set of rows.
limitation: A two-class assignment assumes that the objects to be assigned are already specified.
distance: In the uplink the rows represent selected pairs, so exact assignment restores distinct tones without certifying that the partners were globally optimal.

authors: 3GPP
title: Study on channel model for frequencies from 0.5 to 100 GHz
contribution: The report defines channel models and scenario parameters for radio-system evaluation across 0.5–100 GHz.
strength: Its specified delay, angular and fading distributions support reproducible channel draws.
limitation: A stochastic model supplies a distribution for simulations and cannot establish performance in a particular physical deployment.
distance: The simulated scheduling intervals apply to realizations of the chosen profiles and their specified parameters.

authors: Hoydis, J. et al.
title: Sionna: an open-source library for next-generation physical layer research
contribution: This software paper describes an open-source, GPU-accelerated framework for link-level physical-layer simulation.
strength: Composable channel and receiver components make large simulation experiments reproducible.
limitation: The library implements selectable models whose physical relevance depends on the scenario and parameters supplied.
distance: Sionna generates simulation inputs for the interval experiments, while the scheduling witnesses are computed separately.

authors: Alkhateeb, A.
title: DeepMIMO: a generic deep learning dataset for millimeter wave and massive MIMO applications
contribution: DeepMIMO constructs parameterized wireless channel datasets from site-specific ray-tracing scenarios.
strength: The scene, array and user choices can be recorded so researchers can reconstruct comparable channel matrices.
limitation: Ray-traced paths inherit the map, propagation assumptions and sampling choices of their scenario.
distance: The uplink study computes bounds for channels drawn from two ray-traced scenes using this dataset framework.

authors: Zafari, M.
title: Distributed Multi-User MIMO Datasets
contribution: This data deposit supplies multiuser uplink recordings from co-located and distributed antenna panels under different synchronization configurations.
strength: Recorded pilots permit comparison of spatial channel estimates across frames on real radios.
limitation: The available captures reflect particular hardware, users, layouts and clock arrangements.
distance: The uplink study derives its recorded-input and later-pilot scheduling comparisons from these waveforms.

authors: Doost-Mohammady, R. et al.
title: RENEW: programmable and observable massive MIMO networks
venue: Proc. 52nd Asilomar Conf. Signals Syst. Comput.
contribution: The RENEW platform exposes a software-defined massive-MIMO radio apparatus for programmable experiments.
strength: Programmability and access to observations support reproducible studies of array processing on hardware.
limitation: A platform description cannot identify the synchronization, user motion or data split of a subsequent recording.
distance: The interval evaluation uses identified captures and decoding conventions from this platform.

authors: Shepard, C., Ding, J., Guerra, R. E. & Zhong, L.
title: Understanding real many-antenna MU-MIMO channels
venue: Proc. 50th Asilomar Conf. Signals Syst. Comput.
contribution: The Argos survey measures multiuser channels over several bands and indoor and outdoor settings with large antenna arrays.
strength: Time-resolved, simultaneous spatial observations expose channel structure suppressed by ideal independent-fading assumptions.
limitation: The campaign covers particular sites, user populations, frequencies and trajectories.
distance: The scheduling study uses selected Argos recordings to measure spatial overlap between channels, which helps explain the interference seen by a paired receiver.

authors: Barnhart, C., Johnson, E. L., Nemhauser, G. L., Savelsbergh, M. W. P. & Vance, P. H.
title: Branch-and-price: column generation for solving huge integer programs
contribution: Branch-and-price combines column generation for a linear relaxation with branching to solve large integer programs.
strength: A pricing subproblem can certify that omitted columns cannot improve the current linear relaxation.
limitation: An integer optimum can still require branching after pricing closes the relaxation.
distance: The uplink calculation instead retains a checkable upper bound when the relaxed matching gives several pairs the same tone.

authors: Matthiesen, B., Hellings, C., Jorswieck, E. A. & Utschick, W.
title: Mixed monotonic programming for fast global optimization
contribution: Matthiesen and colleagues developed mixed monotonic programming for global optimization, with applications including interference-network resource allocation and beamforming.
strength: Exposing monotonicity in the original variables can avoid auxiliary dimensions and nested optimization problems.
limitation: The cost of reaching a requested global tolerance still depends on the bounds and search required for each instance.
distance: Here local two-power box bounds feed a separate matching relaxation, so the achievable-rate interval accounts for both power uncertainty within boxes and competition for tones.

authors: Yu, W. & Lui, R.
title: Dual methods for nonconvex spectrum optimization of multicarrier systems
contribution: Yu and Lui established zero duality gap under a time-sharing condition for nonconvex multicarrier spectrum optimization.
strength: They explain why dual prices can recover an optimum for practical spectrum models in a many-carrier limit.
limitation: The time-sharing condition need not hold for a finite collection of indivisible scheduling resources.
distance: Here an explicit two-tone channel retains a positive relaxation gap at the best tone prices.

authors: Zhao, Y. & Pottie, G. J.
title: Optimal spectrum management in multiuser interference channels
contribution: Zhao and Pottie derived conditions favouring orthogonal access and convexified weighted-sum-rate optimization in continuous-frequency interference channels.
strength: Their analysis connects interference strength to the choice between sharing and separating spectrum.
limitation: The convexification exploits the ability to divide continuous frequency bands.
distance: In the present model each indivisible tone carries a single pair, so two pairs that prefer it must compete for the same label.

authors: Dyer, M. E. & Frieze, A. M.
title: Planar 3DM is NP-complete
contribution: The authors prove that perfect three-dimensional matching remains NP-complete when its incidence graph is planar.
strength: Even a strong restriction on the incidence structure preserves the difficulty of selecting disjoint triples.
limitation: The reduction treats a prescribed family of abstract triples and a yes-or-no covering objective.
distance: A pair and a labelled tone also form a triple, but transferring hardness would require realizing the reduction with feasible channel-derived rates.

authors: Razaviyayn, M., Sanjabi, M. & Luo, Z.-Q.
title: Linear transceiver design for interference alignment: complexity and computation
contribution: The paper proves hardness results for maximizing spatial degrees of freedom and for testing specified degrees of freedom in a MIMO interference channel.
strength: For feasibility it distinguishes hard antenna configurations from a tractable case with at most two antennas per node.
limitation: Its complexity results concern spatial alignment and high-SNR degrees of freedom.
distance: The paired uplink compares finite-SNR rates on labelled tones at one array, so these reductions do not settle the complexity of its oracle.

authors: Salaün, L., Chen, C. S. & Coupechoux, M.
title: Optimal joint subcarrier and power allocation in NOMA is strongly NP-hard
contribution: The authors prove strong NP-hardness for joint subcarrier and power allocation in multicarrier NOMA across several rate utilities.
strength: The result covers weighted sum rate as well as fairness objectives.
limitation: The rate model uses successive interference cancellation and permits allocations governed by the paper’s NOMA constraints.
distance: The present receiver treats its partner as interference and each user appears once, so the NOMA result motivates the comparison without proving a complexity claim for this model.

authors: Hejazi, P., Sabaei, M. & Hajmahmoudi, A.
title: Pilot-efficient channel estimation for 6G MU-mMIMO using LS initialization and GAN-augmented CNN refinement
contribution: Hejazi and colleagues refined least-squares channel estimates with a convolutional network trained on data augmented by a generative adversarial network.
strength: Their ray-traced experiments compare estimation error across pilot budgets and signal-to-noise ratios.
limitation: Normalized mean-square error averages reconstruction performance and does not give a coverage probability for a subsequent scheduling decision.
distance: The present paper calibrates held-out vector and receiver-projection errors and propagates them to an oracle rate ceiling and an achieved-rate floor.

authors: Lei, J., G’Sell, M., Rinaldo, A., Tibshirani, R. J. & Wasserman, L.
title: Distribution-free predictive inference for regression
contribution: The authors develop conformal prediction intervals for regression, including a computationally efficient split procedure.
strength: Exchangeability yields finite-sample marginal coverage without specifying the response distribution.
limitation: Marginal coverage does not ensure conditional coverage for a particular site, clock configuration or selected test case.
distance: The uplink study must choose block scores for full-vector error and error along its deployed receive directions and justify exchangeability of the calibration units.

authors: Johnstone, C. & Cox, B.
title: Conformal uncertainty sets for robust optimization
contribution: Johnstone and Cox construct conformal ellipsoids for robust optimization using a Mahalanobis conformity score.
strength: The experiments compare the coverage and decision quality of Mahalanobis conformal ellipsoids with those of axis-aligned and Gaussian-based uncertainty sets.
limitation: The coverage guarantee is marginal under exchangeability, and the ellipsoid describes the full uncertain vector.
distance: The receiver scheduler calibrates projected errors for its fixed action and full-vector errors for an oracle that can change the receive direction.

authors: Kludze, A., Bodet, D., Jornet, J. M. & Ghasempour, Y.
title: Distributed wavefront shaping in radiative near-field sub-terahertz wireless networks
contribution: Coordinated transmitting apertures extended the range over which near-field wavefront shaping improved a sub-terahertz link.
strength: The authors tested their wave-propagation model experimentally and distinguished the useful focusing range from the nominal Fresnel region.
limitation: Its effective near-field range is defined by the performance advantage of coordinated wavefront shaping under the tested propagation geometry.
distance: The Rice recordings probe the receiver-side consequences of combining spatially distributed observations under different clock configurations.

authors: Shen, R. & Ghasempour, Y.
title: Joint communication and sensing with structured beams carrying orbital angular momentum
contribution: The authors transmitted orthogonal orbital-angular-momentum modes concurrently and varied which modes carried data to obtain different sensing measurements.
strength: Over-the-air measurements at 120 GHz tested data transmission and target localization using the same structured beams.
limitation: The capacity argument assumes the receiver aperture captures the electric fields of the selected modes.
distance: A paired uplink must assess the separability of user channels at its deployed receiver even when the transmitter has imposed no modal structure.

authors: Rogalin, R. et al.
title: Scalable synchronization and reciprocity calibration for distributed multiuser MIMO
contribution: Rogalin and colleagues develop over-the-air protocols for timing and frequency synchronization and reciprocity calibration across distributed access points.
strength: The analysis ties synchronization accuracy to the feasibility of coherent multiuser downlink precoding with separate access-point clocks.
limitation: The protocols address radio alignment for a transmitter that infers downlink channels from uplink pilots.
distance: The uplink replay evaluates filters across recorded pilots under two clock configurations and leaves the separate contributions of timing, frequency and reciprocity errors unresolved.

authors: Vieira, J. et al.
title: Reciprocity calibration for massive MIMO: proposal, modeling, and validation
contribution: Vieira and colleagues use antenna-pair sounding and an expectation-maximization algorithm to estimate base-station reciprocity-calibration coefficients.
strength: Measurements validate the calibration method and reveal frequency structure that can reduce calibration error.
limitation: The calibrated hardware coefficients support downlink precoding from uplink channel estimates.
distance: The scheduler instead tests the achieved uplink rate of a frozen filter and treats changes between recorded pilots as observable prediction errors.

authors: Ganesan, U. K., Sarvendranath, R. & Larsson, E. G.
title: BeamSync: over-the-air synchronization for distributed massive MIMO systems
contribution: Ganesan and colleagues derive a beamformed over-the-air protocol for estimating phase and frequency offsets between distributed access points.
strength: They establish when phase calibration of reciprocity-calibrated access points suffices for coherent transmission and identify the optimal inter-access-point beam direction.
limitation: The method assumes an active synchronization exchange between radios.
distance: The recorded uplink comparison observes the effects present under shared and local clocks without estimating the contribution of each impairment.

authors: Zhang, C. et al.
title: Sub-picosecond synchronized multi-faceted fronthaul with one-sample-per-symbol coherent detection
contribution: The authors used bidirectional optical pilots to compensate for delay drift in a fibre link carrying data and a clock reference to a remote radio unit.
strength: They measured the time difference between central and remote clocks with feedback enabled and disabled across a 10 km link under different thermal conditions.
limitation: The measured timing stability depends on bidirectional pilot exchange and an active delay-compensation loop over the fibre link.
distance: The Rice recordings address how a fixed receiver evaluated on a later pilot behaves under shared and local clock configurations.

authors: Ni, Z. et al.
title: Fully-connected microwave photonic multi-beamformer with fast beam-steering for broadband wireless communication
contribution: A broadband photonic beamformer let every element of an eight-element transmit array contribute to each simultaneous beam.
strength: At 13.1 GHz the fully connected configuration delivered a 2.9 dB received-signal gain over partial connectivity with the same array.
limitation: The communication experiment uses transmitted beams with prescribed directions and measures the received downlink waveform.
distance: The paired-uplink analysis holds the receive directions fixed when evaluating the rate of an implemented action.

authors: Dezső, B., Jüttner, A. & Kovács, P.
title: LEMON – an open source C++ graph template library
contribution: The software paper presents C++ graph and network algorithms and their underlying data structures.
strength: An established graph library makes the matching component independently implementable.
limitation: Library benchmarks concern graph primitives and omit the construction and verification of wireless rate bounds.
distance: The uplink implementation uses LEMON to obtain a matching and checks a witness against the edge weights it actually supplied.
